title: Unknown utility crossing
scenario: A proposed storm line crosses an existing gas utility. The plan location is approximate and the depth is not confirmed.
question: What is the best estimating assumption before treating the crossing as straightforward excavation?

options.text: Include controlled daylighting or vacuum excavation to confirm the utility before the crossing work.
Assume the utility is exactly where the plan line is drawn and price normal excavation only.
Ignore the existing utility because it is outside the new pipe quantity.
Increase asphalt quantity to cover the uncertainty.

explanation: Existing utility drawings can be approximate. A controlled exposure can confirm horizontal position and depth before excavation near the crossing.

title: Late tender revision
scenario: A formal tender revision arrives two days before bid closing and changes several drawing details.
question: What should the estimator do first?

options.text: Review the addendum against the current takeoff and pricing, then revise affected quantities and scope before submission.
Keep the original estimate because the takeoff is already complete.
Only save the document for the project manager after award.
Apply a general contingency without checking what changed.

explanation: An addendum is part of the tender documents. Its changes can affect quantities, scope, subcontractor quotes and bid forms.

title: Pipe trench quantities
scenario: A pipe trench detail shows specified bedding below the pipe, compacted material at the haunches and general backfill above.
question: How should the takeoff be structured?

options.text: Measure bedding, haunching and backfill separately because they can use different materials, placement methods and unit costs.
Measure the entire trench volume as one backfill item.
Measure only pipe length because trench materials are incidental.
Combine bedding with asphalt restoration because both are granular work.

explanation: Separating trench zones gives a cleaner quantity and cost build-up, especially where material specifications and production differ.

title: Measured tender item
scenario: A tender item will be paid by the actual measured quantity installed, using the contractor's bid rate per metre.
question: Which pricing approach best matches this bid structure?

options.text: Build a complete cost per metre, including the resources and production needed for one unit of work.
Enter one total project price and ignore the measured quantity.
Price only material because labour will be adjusted later.
Use the contingency amount as the unit rate.

explanation: A unit-price item needs a defensible cost per measured unit. Quantity changes can then extend against the same bid rate.

title: Crew output assumption
scenario: A trench crew is priced for ten working days, but the takeoff quantity and assumed daily output imply fifteen days of work.
question: What should be checked before finalizing the estimate?

options.text: Reconcile the quantity, crew production rate and duration so the labour and equipment hours match the planned output.
Keep the ten-day duration because production does not affect cost.
Reduce the takeoff quantity until it matches the schedule.
Remove equipment hours and keep only labour hours.

explanation: Production connects quantity to time. If quantity divided by daily output does not match the priced duration, the estimate needs reconciliation.

title: Known scope, unknown exact value
scenario: The tender clearly requires a small specialty item, but the supplier price is not available before closing.
question: What is the cleaner estimating treatment?

options.text: Carry a clearly identified allowance for that known scope and document what it covers.
Hide the amount inside general contingency without identifying the scope.
Exclude the item because the supplier has not quoted it yet.
Replace the item with a production rate.

explanation: An allowance can represent a known requirement whose exact cost is not yet established. Contingency is broader risk reserve, not a substitute for documenting known scope.

title: Duct bank takeoff
scenario: A concrete-encased conduit run crosses paved and unpaved areas and includes several structures along the alignment.
question: Which takeoff approach is strongest for estimating?

options.text: Break out conduit, concrete encasement, excavation, backfill, structures and surface restoration so each cost driver is visible.
Use only the duct bank centreline length and one blended material price.
Measure asphalt only because the electrical subcontractor covers everything underground.
Count conduits but ignore concrete and excavation quantities.

explanation: Duct bank cost is driven by more than centreline length. Separating major components makes production, subcontractor scope and restoration easier to review.

title: Road restoration limit
scenario: A road restoration detail requires removal of the existing asphalt surface before a new overlay is placed over the repair area.
question: Which quantities should be checked separately?

options.text: Measure the milling area and the new overlay area separately, then verify whether their limits and thicknesses are actually the same.
Use only the trench width for both operations without reviewing the restoration detail.
Measure milling as excavation volume in cubic metres only.
Ignore milling because overlay automatically includes removal of existing asphalt.

explanation: Removal and replacement are distinct operations. Their limits can differ, so each should be measured from the applicable detail or plan.
